justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon reflect the best guess for the future value based on available data, historical trends, and any relevant model assumptions. In this case, I kept the point estimate the same across all horizons—226.24—because it represents a stable central tendency derived from recent observations. This suggests that, in the absence of strong evidence to the contrary, I expect the value to remain around this level in the short term, one week out, and even one month out. The assumption here is that any changes over time will be small and centered around this baseline.

The width of the confidence intervals broadens as the forecast horizon increases because uncertainty naturally grows the further we look into the future. Over one day, there's less time for unexpected events or variability to affect the outcome, so the confidence interval (222.71 to 229.77) is relatively narrow. By one week, there's more room for volatility, leading to a wider range (218.5 to 234.01). At the one-month mark, even more uncertainty accumulates due to potential unforeseen factors, so the interval expands further (211.0 to 241.48). These include not just the inherent randomness of the system but also potential shifts in underlying conditions or external shocks to the system.

There are always risks or events that might push outcomes outside the stated ranges. For instance, specific unforeseen events such as major news releases, regulatory changes, geopolitical disruptions, or sudden economic shocks could create drastic shifts beyond what historical patterns alone would predict. For the one-month horizon in particular, a highly volatile or unusual event could drive the value well beyond the established confidence interval, as the forecast assumes a relatively stable system and may not fully account for rare or extreme scenarios. This highlights why it’s always important to communicate the limitations of forecasts—they are built on probabilities, not certainties.
